groups.title: Evolution and climate change

questions.prompt: According to the passage, all of the following can contribute to a species' ability to adapt to climate change EXCEPT:

options.text: Large population with a wide range of genetic traits.
Interbreeding with closely related species.
Short term habitat shifts and changes in activity times.
Small populations, long generations and fewer mutations.

questions.prompt: Which of the following examples best compares with the rapid adaptation of Atlantic killifish in polluted environments?

options.text: Tropical forests expanding their range into temperate zones due to global warming.
Coral reefs altering their symbiotic relationships to survive warmer ocean temperatures.
Bacteria developing resistance to a broad spectrum of antibiotics due to genetic mutations.
Mountain species migrating to higher elevations to maintain their climate preferences.

questions.prompt: Which of the following plant adaptation techniques does NOT align with the ‘rainbowfish species’ example in the passage?

options.text: Boosting the capacity for photosynthesis in plant species to absorb more CO2.
Conservation through introduction of genetic material to at-risk plant species.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the most effective conservation strategy for sea turtles would be:

options.text: Moving sea turtles to cooler waters to reduce global warming impact.
Creating climate-resistant genetically modified sea turtles.
Managing nesting beaches for diverse incubation temperatures.

groups.stimulus:
As the world changes, flora and fauna must adapt to shifting habitats and climates. With climate change accelerating environmental shifts, a key question emerges: Can evolution keep pace? According to evolutionary ecologist Sarah Diamond, many species surprisingly can adapt quickly. Traditionally viewed as a slow process, recent research reveals that evolution can match the rapid timelines of climate change. Scientists are investigating what drives evolutionary adaptation to identify how species can adapt to rapid planetary changes.

In their review, Diamond and her team compile research on the rapid evolution of climate-relevant traits like heat tolerance and resistance to dryness or ocean acidification. Their analysis uncovers promising findings, including a lab experiment demonstrating that Chlorella vulgaris, a type of green algae, can quickly adapt to temperatures 3 degrees Celsius above its optimal range. Andrew Whitehead, who studies evolution and genomics at the University of California, Davis, says the species with the best chances of navigating the changes to come are those with large and genetically diverse populations. “Genetic variation is fuel for evolutionary change, and some [species] have more of that fuel than others," he says.

Whitehead's research reveals that Atlantic killifish have adapted to heavily polluted estuaries thanks to their vast genetic diversity, the highest among vertebrates. Their large populations and short generations result in numerous mutations, some of which enable survival in harsh conditions. The key to adapting to rapid challenges like climate change lies in a species' existing genetic diversity, as new mutations can't wait to emerge, notes Whitehead. Species with a broader genetic "deck" have a better chance of having the "lucky cards" necessary for adaptation. While most species have less genetic variety than some highly adaptable ones, hybridization with closely related species could enhance their genetic repertoire, allowing them to acquire needed traits faster, according to molecular ecologist Luciano Beheregaray.

In Australian rivers, closely related rainbowfish species adapt to climate change through hybridization. Cold-adapted fish from higher elevations mate with warm-adapted ones from lower areas, creating hybrids more resilient to warming. Beheregaray highlights this hybrid vigor as a means of enhancing adaptability, suggesting that humans could intervene by introducing beneficial genetic material to at-risk populations, offering a proactive approach to conservation over passive observation of extinction. Even if animals don't have the genetic diversity or hybridization potential to weather the coming warming, there are other ways they can adapt, says Ryan Martin, one of Diamond's Case Western colleagues who also studies evolutionary responses to climate change. Some animals can move, seeking out microhabitats that remain in their preferred temperature range, he says. Or they can adjust their behavior to be more active at cooler times of the day, which might buffer them against the effects of climate change.

Behavioral adaptations, like moving to cooler areas, have limits; animals can't escape indefinitely, and evolving new tolerances takes time, Martin notes. Diamond predicts a drastic change in animal communities due to climate warming, with large marine animals and species with temperature-dependent sex determination, like sea turtles, facing extinction risks. In contrast, adaptable species such as squid and copepods may thrive. The outcome will highlight clear “winners and losers," with significant losses among well-known species.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements best describes the significance of the 18th century in the history of aesthetic philosophy?

options.text: It marked the period when aesthetic experiences were first linked with divine beauty.

It represented a shift of focus from divine beauty to sensory and personal experience.

groups.stimulus:
Any aesthetic experience has intentionality: it is an experience (as) of some object. Typically, that object will be a work of art or some aspect of nature. An aesthetic experience of an object with sensible features is commonly thought to be a perceptual experience of those sensible features. In the case of poems, ... and certain pieces of conceptual art, the experience might be understood as an imagined sensory experience; in the case of abstract or intelligible objects like theorems, it might be neither sensory nor imaginative in nature.

It is common to individuate aesthetic experience partly in terms of the types of properties on which this experience focuses. In perceiving a sculpture, you might experience its shape, its color, its resemblance to a real person, its placement in a gallery, its authorship, or its representational style.

Long before the 18th-century development of special theories of aesthetic experience, neo-Platonic medieval philosophers developed a concept of beauty as rationally intelligible formal structure as it could be appreciated in experience. In his fourth-century work De Musica, Augustine took beauty in music to be partly a matter of proportionality of parts, and later argued that visual beauty is formal harmony combined in the right way with color. Nine centuries later, Thomas Aquinas echoed this hylomorphic conception: the beautiful is material structured in proper form, the kind “of which apprehension in itseIf pleases” In the Italian Renaissance, Leon Battista Alberti called beauty “reasoned harmony of all the parts within a body:”

In the eighteenth century, attention to aesthetic experience per se, rather than beauty, grew out of a more general inquiry into perception. Alexander Baumgarten first defined “aesthetics” much more broadly as we do now—as the science of cognizing objects by sensory perception. ...

These early claims that experience of beauty is experience of form were thoroughly integrated into the general theistic metaphysics and epistemology of these thinkers. Baumgarten, for instance, claimed that we take pleasure not only in the perfection of an object, he wrote, but also in being conscious of our own “perfection of sensible cognition as such; in how we are suited to sense the world. The contemporary English philosopher Anthony Ashbury Cooper, took pleasurable admiration of well-formed objects really to be admiration of the form- imposing minds, including those of the artist but ultimately that of the divine. “The beautifying, not the beautified, is the really beautiful” he wrote.

Immanuel Kant's immensely influential Critique of Judgment peeled aesthetic experience away from apprehension of the divine, and cleaved the apprehension of form away from function. He claimed you make a pure judgment of “free” beauty when you take pleasure just in perceiving the form of an object without even conceptualizing its function.

Kant disputes his German predecessors by asserting that beauty and perfection are independent, but he makes concessions: first, he acknowledges they may have confused objective perfection with subjective purposiveness, which relates to the harmonious arrangement of an object's parts in the imagination. Secondly, he admits that we sometimes attribute “accessory beauty" to objects that perfectly fulfill their function, like a well-designed building.

groups.title: Antimatter and gravity

questions.prompt: According to the passage, The CERN experiment:

options.text: Confirmed Galileo's prediction that gravity might repel antimatter.
Demonstrated the annihilation of antihydrogen under gravity.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following sets of words/phrases best serves as keywords to the passage?

options.text: Antigravity, Antihydrogen, Matter Annihilation, Spatial Separation
Antimatter, Gravitational Forces, Antihydrogen, CERN Experiment

questions.prompt: Which of the following CANNOT be inferred from the passage?

questions.prompt: In light of the passage’s context, which states, “The next step is to measure the acceleration as precisely as we can,’ if precise measurements reveal that the acceleration due to gravity for antimatter is identical to that for matter, which concept mentioned in the passage would be most seriously challenged?

options.text: Galileo's foundational principles of gravity.
The Big Bang theory and the origins of the universe.
The theory of spatial separation between matter and antimatter.
Gravity's relative weakness compared to other natural forces.

groups.stimulus:
Galileo put gravitational theory to the test by dropping balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa. Four hundred years on, scientists have performed a higher tech version of the experiment to demonstrate for the first time that antimatter also falls downwards. The study, by scientists at CERN, showed conclusively that gravity pulls antihydrogen downwards and that, at least for antimatter, antigravity does not exist. “Broadly speaking, we're making antimatter and we're doing a Leaning Tower of Pisa kind of experiment,’ said Prof Jonathan Wurtele, a theoretical physicist at the University of California, Berkeley. “We're letting the antimatter go, and we're seeing if it goes up or down”

Antimatter is a mirror version of ordinary matter, with some basic properties like electrical charge reversed. Antiprotons have the same mass, but a negative charge, while antielectrons (also called positrons) are positively charged. When matter and antimatter meet, they annihilate each other and produce energy, meaning that in a matter-dominated world like our own, antimatter only fleetingly comes into existence. But most theories predict that equal amounts of matter and antimatter should have been produced during the big bang, and the mystery of what happened to all the antimatter is a central question in fundamental physics.

For some, the concept of antigravity has been an enticing potential explanation to this conundrum. This could have led to the spatial separation of matter and antimatter in the early universe, meaning that we only see a small amount of antimatter in the local universe. There are other theoretical reasons that make this idea unlikely, but as the question had never been put to the test, it had remained a fringe possibility. “Until you measure it, you just don’t know. That's science,” said Jeffrey Hangst, a particle physicist at Aarhus University, Denmark, and spokesperson of the Antihydrogen Laser Physics Apparatus (Alpha) collaboration at CERN.

A direct measurement of antimatter falling is hugely challenging because the gravitational force is so weak compared with the other three known forces of nature and scientists have struggled to preserve antimatter for long enough to carry out experiments. The latest study, published in Nature, used antihydrogen atoms cooled to haIf a degree above absolute zero (-273.15C). About 100 of the antimatter atoms were confined in a 25 cm-long magnetic bottle with an opening at the top and bottom. Meticulous measurements showed that the atoms were more likely to escape, and meet their annihilation, at the bottom of the bottle due to gravitational forces.

The gravitational acceleration was found to be within 25% of normal gravity, meaning that it could be identical to the gravitational force experienced by ordinary matter - or at least, similar. “It has taken us 30 years to learn how to make this anti-atom, to hold onto it, and to control it well enough that we could actually drop it in a way that it would be sensitive to the force of gravity,” said Hangst. “The next step is to measure the acceleration as precisely as we can.”

questions.prompt: As described in the passage, brain-machine interface (BMI) implants are designed to assist individuals with all the following conditions EXCEPT:

options.text: Brain damage from strokes, tumors, injuries, or substance abuse.
Locked-in syndrome, where the person is conscious but paralyzed and non-verbal.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which of the following is NOT an implication of the discovery that the supramarginal gyrus (SMG) in the parietal lobe is involved in speech?

options.text: A potential reevaluation of the brain's functional map.
Improved understanding and treatment of muscular disorders.
Enhanced development of BMIs for speech restoration.
Innovations in diagnosing and treating speech disorders.

questions.prompt: In the comparison, “brain-machine interface (and) a football game." the role of the implanted device is that of:

questions.prompt: Based on the experiment involving tetraplegic patients, which of the following CANNOT be validly inferred about the participants in the study?

options.text: They were fully conscious and able to understand the instructions.
They had intact cognitive functions to think of specific words.
They had intact sensory function of either hearing or vision.
They could later confirm the accuracy of BMI’s decoding of thoughts.

groups.stimulus:
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Alexander Dumas's depiction of a condition where "the soul is trapped in a non-responsive body” is an early account of locked-in syndrome, a severe paralysis from brain stem damage due to strokes, tumors, injuries, snakebites, substance abuse, infections, or diseases like ALS.

The advent of brain-machine interfaces (BMIs) offer hope for restoring communication in locked-in individuals by using implanted devices to translate brain waves associated with intended speech into messages, without the need for blinking, eye tracking, or vocal attempts, directly conveying silent thoughts into words or letters. Sarah Wandelt at the California Institute of Technology notes the significant potential of brain-machine interfaces to aid those completely unable to communicate. Research, including Wandelt's, shows these interfaces can decode internal speech, though they are invasive, costly, and need extensive development to offer locked-in patients a way to communicate.

Choosing a brain area is the first step in creating a brain-machine interface. Historical beliefs in phrenology, which mapped mental faculties to skull contours, are now dismissed as inaccurate. Modern neuroscience, as David Bjanes notes, understands mental functions as arising from complex interactions across brain regions within neural networks. This complexity means that multiple areas could be potential targets for tapping into internal language, presenting both challenges and opportunities for interface development. Wandelt, Bjanes, and colleagues discovered that the supramarginal gyrus (SMG) in the parietal lobe, known for its role in object manipulation, also activates during speech. This was found using a microelectrode array implanted in a tetraplegic participant's SMG to record neuron activity, transmitting data for processing. Bjanes compares their brain-machine interface to a football game, with the brain as the stadium and neurons as spectators. Electrodes act as microphones to capture the "voices" of key players (neurons) to interpret the game's actions, aiming to decode brain activity for clearer communication through the device.

Implanted brain devices monitor electrochemical signals between neurons, translating them into audio-like patterns for different actions or thoughts. The Caltech team's interface, after minimal training, could accurately identify spoken and invented words by a tetraplegic participant with over 90% accuracy, using a basic algorithm. Presented by Wandelt at the 2022 Society for Neuroscience conference, this study, though preliminary, demonstrates the interface's potential to significantly aid communication, suggesting that expanding the vocabulary could greatly benefit locked-in patients. An alternative brain-machine interface design recognizes letters, allowing patients to spell words by mouthing each letter's code, enabling full sentence communication. Sean Metzger notes this mimics spelling over noisy phone lines, with NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., Alpha for A) enhancing clarity. In a study with a stroke patient using an electrode array covering a large motor cortex area, researchers decoded 92% of silently spelled sentences using machine learning. Metzger suggests combining this letter-based method with a previous word-based approach could streamline communication, making it faster and less taxing for users.

The main hurdle in restoring speech for locked-in patients lies in the biological variability of how speech is internally encoded, which can differ by individual or context. People might visualize, hear, or associate words differently, leading to unique brain wave patterns for the same words across individuals.

groups.title: Game of numbers

questions.prompt: If Prasad announces the values of A and B as 4 and 2 respectively, how many pairs of numbers formed by Prasad in his mind can satisfy these values of A and B?
If Prasad announces the values of A and B as 0 and 0 respectively, how many pairs of numbers formed by Prasad in his mind can satisfy these values of A and B?
If Prasad announces the values of A and B as 1 and 0 respectively, how many pairs of numbers formed by Prasad in his mind can satisfy these values of A and B?
If Prasad announces the values of A and B as 4 and 0 respectively, how many pairs of numbers formed by Prasad in his mind can satisfy these values of A and B?
If Prasad announces the values of A and B as 3 and 1 respectively, how many pairs of numbers formed by Prasad in his mind can satisfy these values of A and B?

groups.stimulus:
Prakash, Prashant and Prasad are playing a game called ‘Game of numbers’ In the game, Prakash and Prashant initially take a four digit number (without repetition of the digits, not involving 0). The numbers taken by the two may or may not be equal. Both Prakash and Prashant individually tell their numbers to Prasad. However, Prakash and Prashant do not know the numbers taken by each other.

On hearing the two numbers, Prasad forms an ordered pair of the two numbers in his mind and announces the following:

The number of digits common between the numbers taken by Prakash and Prashant. (Prasad calls this ‘A’)

The number of common digits between the numbers taken by Prakash and Prashant at the same places. (Prasad calls this ‘B’)

For example, if Prakash and Prashant take numbers 1947 and 1857 respectively, Prasad announces the values of A and B both as 2. This is because there are two digits common between the two numbers (1 and 7) and both the digits are at the same places (thousands and unit’s places respectively). In this example, (1947, 1857) is the pair formed by Prasad in his mind. Since this is an ordered pair, (1857, 1947) is not the same pair as (1947, 1857). Similarly, if Prakash and Prashant take numbers 3829 and 8176 respectively, Prasad announces the values of A and B are 1 and 0 respectively. This is because there is one digit common between the two numbers (8) but the common digit does not occupy the same places in the two numbers. In this example, (3829,8176) is the pair formed by Prasad in his mind. Since this is an ordered pair, (8176, 3829) is not the same pair as (3829,8176).

groups.stimulus: Shakunimama has a unique 10-faced die, which is in the shape of an octagonal prism. The die consists of two parallel regular octagon shaped surfaces and eight identical rectangular surfaces that are perpendicular to the octagonal surfaces. The eight rectangular surfaces consist of four pairs of surfaces that are parallel to each other, as shown in the following figure. First ten natural numbers are written on the ten surfaces of the die such that each surface has exactly one number written on it. Out of the 8 rectangular surfaces, the surfaces denoted by ‘a’, ‘b’ ‘c’ and ‘d’ are called ‘South surfaces’ and the remaining 4 rectangular surfaces are called ‘North surfaces’. The sum of the numbers written on the ‘South surfaces’ is equal to the sum of the numbers written on the ‘North surfaces’. Similarly, the sum of the numbers written on each pair of the parallel surfaces is equal. We denote the quadruple of the numbers written on the ‘South surfaces’ in the ascending order as the ‘South set’.

Wallace was assassinated on 22nd November 1963, after which his Vice President, Curtis was immediately sworn in as the President. 2. Barkley resigned from the post of President on 9th August 1974, after which his Vice President, Rockefeller was immediately sworn in as the President. 3. Agnew passed away at the age 94 on 30th November 2018, while Nixon passed away on 28th March 1969 at the age 79. 4. Quale, Cheney, Gore and Humphrey are the only living former Presidents. 5. Former Presidents Curtis, Barkley, Bush and Rockefeller passed away in the same chronological order. They lived for 65, 81, 93 and 83 years respectively.

questions.prompt: A, B and C are three friends who make earthen pots. A is 25% more efficient than B and B is 30% more efficient than C. If they work alone, each of them manufactures integral number of pots per day. As B and C are very good friends they chat a lot during the time they work together and as a result their productivity reduces by 25%. A has no such problem and always maintains his productivity at the same level. How many pots are produced by B & C together in a day if they produce 8 pots more than A per day?

Three containers v1, v2, and v3 are containing solution of water and chocolate syrup in the ratio of 3: 2,4:3, and 3:5 respectively. In which of the following ratios can we mix solutions v1, v2, and v3 to get a resultant solution with more than 50% concentration of water?

Aman goes to fruit market to purchase apple, banana and mango. Fruits are sold at fixed rate per piece. Aman purchases 9 apples, 25 bananas, and 4 mangoes. Had he bought 4 more bananas instead of buying 4 mangoes, he could have reduced his expenditure by 26%. However, had he bought 9 more bananas instead of buying 9 apples, he could have reduced his expenditure by 36%. How much the expenditure would reduce in percentage if he had bought 38 bananas only?

(iii) Average number of chocolates with Rupal, Amit and Yash was 36. What must be the average of number of chocolates with Rupal, Harsh, Amit and Yash now?
